source.title: Pretraining on the Test Set Is All You Need

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neural scaling laws and presents a satirical claim about training loss, but does not measure the held-out loss or other outcomes specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper states that phi-CTNL's pretraining bits per word falls faster than power-law scaling as epochs increase. This is a training-loss measure, not stated to be held-out loss, so it does not test a listed version. Figure 1 benchmark numbers are explicitly said possibly to be made up, and the paper estimates 100% evaluation-data contamination; it provides no scaling or predictability result relevant to the listed versions. Cited scaling-law results are not the paper's own results.
record.test_reason: Self-declared satire. The only scaling-like result is training bits per word versus epochs for one 1M-parameter model trained on test benchmarks (Fig. 2 left). That is training loss on repeated data, not held-out loss across parameters, tokens or compute. No fits, sweeps or downstream-predictability results are reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The paper is satire. The author's point is that boastful benchmark claims made without checking for evaluation-data contamination undermine the field. It draws no genuine conclusion about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: No reproduction or comparison of the original scaling-law methods is reported.

fits_no_version.finding: Training bits per word of a 1M model trained on benchmark test data falls rapidly toward zero with epochs (memorisation), which the satire calls 'faster-than-power-law'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training loss on a tiny, fully memorisable corpus can fall faster than a power law in epochs; this is overfitting, not held-out scaling.

record.problems: The paper identifies itself as satire. Figure 2 provides no numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The paper says Figure 1 numbers might have been made up and estimates 100% evaluation-data contamination.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The benchmark comparisons and canary example do not test the listed scaling or downstream-predictability versions.

untested.parts: All: no held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation from small-run fits.
All: no other modalities or regimes; repeated-epoch training loss on test data does not count.
All: benchmark scores come from contamination, with no scale trend; Figure 1 numbers 'might have been made up'.
All: no comparison of fits or setups.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6 and 'discusses' are appropriate; the paper only cites scaling-law work as a target of parody. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out loss; scaling against parameter count, tokens, or compute with the other factors not bottlenecking.
No small-run fits or comparison with larger runs.
No compute-budget allocation sweep over parameter and token counts.
No architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.
No tests in other modalities or training regimes.
No test of predictable downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or optimal allocations across setups or fitting choices.

rows.subject: phi-CTNL
rows.operation_detail: Reports pretraining bits per word across pretraining epochs and describes the result as faster than power-law scaling with compute.
rows.note: The text says the value rapidly falls toward zero and calls it faster than predicted under power-law scaling. It does not say this is held-out loss; the paper identifies itself as satire.
rows.check: Training loss of a single model across epochs of memorised test data. It is not held-out loss scaling across parameters, data or compute. Values are figure-only, and the 'beats power law' framing is satirical.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
